post_message: Vaccines not only save lives — they change them. Vaccine-preventable diseases can cause school absences, lost wages, birth defects, and overburdened health systems.  Continuing to develop new vaccines, removing barriers to access, countering misinformation, and advocating for vaccine equity are critical to helping all communities realize the full benefits of immunization. #VaccinesWork

Our Research & Development team has many scientists with unique backgrounds coming together to create new vaccines. 💪  At Sabin, we advance strong vaccine candidates for diseases like Marburg and Sudan virus, which often lack commercial interest and disproportionately affect the world’s most vulnerable populations.

In some parts of the world, vaccination can seem like a secondary concern as parents grapple with other tough issues. As one mother told Angu Glory, Cameroon Baptist Convention Health Services (CBCHS) Project District Officer: “There is no need for the vaccine because hunger will kill my child before any vaccine-preventable disease does.”  That comment reflects the harsh reality caregivers in this region face. “Families aren’t rejecting vaccines. They’re frustrated and overwhelmed by the daily struggles to survive,” Glory said.   Recognizing this issue, health workers in the area sought to improve vaccine uptake while helping families meet those additional needs.   The impact was immediate More than 160,000 children were vaccinated, more than 68,000 were screened for malnutrition, over 1,000 received mosquito nets, and more than 13,000 caregivers received practical education on nutrition and vaccines.  Read the full story at the link in our bio.

Recently published research from Sabin finds robust influenza vaccination systems can play an important role in pandemic preparedness, notes co-author Marissa Malchione.   Sabin looked at seasonal influenza programs in five middle-income countries and found strong seasonal flu programs keep the people, systems, supply chains, and public trust intact to be ready before the next pandemic.
